title: Predictive care for energy workers | Wood Mackenzie
gist: In this Energy Gang podcast summary, Ed Crooks talks with neuroscientist and AI entrepreneur Olivier Oullier about 'predictive care'. The idea is that neuroadaptive AI reads brainwaves, facial expression, eye movement and voice to detect fatigue or overload in energy workers, extending predictive maintenance from equipment to people. Oullier says pilots are running in Mexico, Australia and the UAE, while the episode weighs the surveillance and consent risks and looks ahead to world models for physical AI.

insights.claim: Olivier Oullier argues AI can improve energy operator safety and productivity at once through neuroadaptive systems that use brainwaves, facial expression, eye movement and voice to detect fatigue, stress, distraction or cognitive overload.
insights.so_what: A new industrial-AI category for worker safety in energy operations.
insights.locator: Host Ed Crooks is joined by Olivier Oullier
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks

insights.claim: Neuroadaptive systems in energy operations could adapt control-room dashboards to show the information that matters most, or help collaborative robots respond when an operator is tired or distracted.

insights.claim: Drawing on lessons from surgery and transport, Oullier frames human monitoring as an extension of predictive maintenance, moving from monitoring equipment to anticipating human needs, which he calls predictive care.
insights.so_what: Energy firms' existing sensor/AI infrastructure could extend to worker monitoring.

insights.claim: Continuous physiological monitoring of energy workers could make work safer but raises concerns about consent, autonomy and employee surveillance; Oullier says such programs should be voluntary, transparent and compliant with regulation.
insights.so_what: Regulatory and labor pushback is the main adoption risk for worker-monitoring AI.
insights.locator: That promise rests on a sensitive trade-off
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks

insights.claim: Oullier points to world models, which aim to help robots understand and act in physical environments, as the next phase of physical AI, while cautioning against precise long-range predictions about AI's impact on jobs.
insights.so_what: World models are a theme to watch for industrial robotics.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks

insights.claim: As AI moves from screens into robots, control rooms and industrial sites, the episode flags poorly supervised AI agents as a risk, and says the near-term challenge for energy companies is to deploy systems that improve safety and performance without losing sight of the people they serve.
insights.so_what: Governance of AI agents in industrial settings is a growing operational risk.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
